variant: Geometry is for the original Wheeler Express FT (cruciform tail, fixed tricycle gear) as measured by CAFE on N360EZ (Continental IO-360-ES1B 210 hp, completed 1995, tested Sept 1997). Express 2000 FT / Series 90 / Auriga share wing and fuselage but use a larger conventional low-set tail (13 ft span stabilizer, ~40% more wetted area than the Express's tail) and typically IO-540 engines and more fuel; no first-hand Express 2000 FT geometry was found.

vtail.note: Highly swept fin with mid-mounted stabilizer (cruciform). CAFE gives only rudder: 52 in span, 4.33 sq ft, chord 12/12 in; fin span/area 'na, symmetric section'. Rudder travel 26 deg per manual (20 deg allowed); CAFE found 20 deg much better. Static height of aircraft 84 in (CAFE). Series 90 claimed 'a 20% larger tail' (Wikipedia Express Series 90, AeroCrafter).

cabin_width.note: CAFE: 44 in at shoulders, 43 in at hips; AeroCrafter via Wikipedia: 46 in

fuselage.note: Glasair-style composite (E-glass/vinyl ester, polyurethane foam core), fuselage split top/bottom; 74 in from front seatbacks to baggage bulkhead; 48x34 in gull-wing door on right side. Overall height 84 in static (CAFE); S2000 height 8 ft (aeropedia).

cooling: air; 2 pitot inlets, downdraft; stock cowl inlet area 47.5 sq in; outlet 35 sq in with electric cowl flap fully open; N360EZ had an enclosed 'doghouse' plenum. safety.pattern: RECORD: Of 13 fatal accidents, about 9 are stall or loss of control in flight: 1990 N210EX spin en route (SEA90FA146); 2015 N3FC stall then spin in a steep turn, where the NTSB named the design ('poor yaw stability at low airspeed') as a contributing factor (CEN15FA321); 2016 N176PA (Series 90) steep takeoff climb then loss of control (WPR17FA041); 2017 N246TM stall in the traffic pattern (WPR17FA185); 2019 N625J (Series 2000) loss of control while maneuvering (ERA19FA154); 2019 N43FD (Series 2000) stall on final (WPR19FA212); 2020 N772BM stall in the departure turn (CEN21LA096); 2022 N44508 (turbine 2000RG) stall after engine fire (CEN22FA216); 2009 Bahamas loss of control. Non-fatal events of the same kind: 2004 Oshawa stall on a go-around with a wing drop near 90 deg (N625J, Series 2000); 2024 Chicoutimi loss of control just after takeoff. Other causes: engine failure or power loss (1989, 2007, 2015 Greeley, 2020), fuel exhaustion or contamination, and nose or main gear collapses (1997 VH-PNK, 2015, 2016). The CAFE 1997 test of N360EZ found low yaw damping (4-5 overshoots), an uncommanded right yaw after 1 g clean stalls with too little elevator until 85 kt, the fin blanking the stabilizer at high yaw so the elevator ran out, and pitot-static errors of 14 kt (reading low near the stall). A 92-gal tank tempts pilots into full-fuel, high-weight operation. INFERENCE: the stall/LOC share is high for a 4-seat single. Low-speed directional problems with the cruciform tail are documented. But several of the stall/LOC fatalities were Series 90/2000 aircraft with the bigger conventional tail, so the tail change alone does not appear to have cured the problem. Wing loading of 22-28 psf on a laminar NLF wing, heavy IO-540 conversions and aft-c.g. loading are plausible co-factors, but we have not verified them.

why_died_detail: Per CAFE (1997): the 1990 fatal demonstrator crash right before Oshkosh caused 'a severe contraction in sales', and Ken Wheeler went bankrupt. The business then passed through Express Design Inc. (Dave Ulrich, Redmond OR, 1992-95; Chapter 7 on 6 Jan 1996 per the Express Link newsletter cited by Wikipedia), Express Aircraft Co. LLC (Olson/Fagerstrom, Olympia WA, 1997; later under Exosphere; assets sold through bankruptcy court) and Composite Aircraft Technology (Darrell Peterson, Toledo WA, Sept 2007). Each bankruptcy left kit builders stranded. Other problems: early plans were incomplete (CAFE says the builder 'created much of the documentation'); build time ran to 2000 hr advertised against 5000 hr actual; only ~30 of ~300 kits were finished by 1997. Handling deficiencies were documented by CAFE and later by the NTSB. The owners' fix for the handling was the larger Series 90/Auriga tail, but stall/LOC fatalities continued in big-tail and heavier IO-540/turbine versions. A revival would need a properly engineered tail and directional stability (fin area, rudder travel limit, stall behavior), honest stall-margin and pitot-static work, and a sound business. A larger tail alone is not supported by the record as a cure.
rights_hints: CAFE 1997: Express Aircraft Company (Larry Olson, Paul Fagerstrom) 'hold the rights to both the Express and the Series 90' (late 1996 purchase). Wikipedia: Composite Aircraft Technology LLC (Darrell Peterson) bought all EAC assets through bankruptcy court in Sept 2007 and moved to Toledo WA (General Aviation News 2009-09-03; EAA page lists CAT at Toledo WA). Checked 2026-10-24: compairtechllc.com now serves an unrelated Chinese-language movie site (domain lapsed) and expressaircraft.com is a parked 'coming soon' page. So CAT's current status and the rights holder are unknown. The 2025 accident aircraft is listed under 'FFF LLC Express 2000 FT'.
